The **2020–21 NBA season** was the 75th season of the National Basketball Association (NBA), though the 75th anniversary was not celebrated until the following season. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the regular season was reduced to 72 games for each team, and began on December 22, 2020.[1] The season started just 72 days after the completion of the 2020 NBA Finals, the shortest off-season in league history.[2] The 2021 NBA All-Star Game was played on March 7, at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, and was won by Team LeBron, 170–150. For the first time, the NBA staged a play-in tournament for teams ranked 7th through 10th in each conference from May 18 to May 21. The playoffs then ran under the standard 16-team playoff format from May 22 to July 20, 2021.[1] Due to COVID-19 cross-border restrictions imposed by the Canadian government, the Toronto Raptors played their 2020–21 home games at Amalie Arena in Tampa, Florida.[3]

In the playoffs, the Rockets defeated the Portland Trail Blazers, 3–1 in the Western Conference First Round.[31][32][33][34] In the Western Conference Semi-finals, the Rockets trailed 0–2 to the Phoenix Suns,[35][36][37] but would win the series in seven games,[38][39][40][41] then defeat the 5th-seeded Utah Jazz, 4–1 in the Western Conference Finals.[42][43][44][45]


In the 1994 NBA Finals, they defeated the New York Knicks in seven games after trailing 3–2,[46][47][48] and won their first championship in franchise history. It was the Rockets' third NBA finals appearance, after 1981 and 1986. Olajuwon was the only player of the 1985–86 Rockets to still be on the 1993–94 team. By winning the Finals MVP, Olajuwon also became the first player to win regular season MVP, Defensive Player of the Year, and Finals MVP in the same season.[49][50][51][52][53] The Rockets also became the first team from the Midwest Division since the Milwaukee Bucks 23 years prior to win the NBA title.

The **1994–95 NBA season** was the Rockets' 28th season in the National Basketball Association, and 24th season in Houston.[1] After winning their first championship, the Rockets went on to win their first nine games of the season. However, with increased competition in the West, management felt a change was needed to win another title. On February 14, 1995, the Rockets traded Otis Thorpe to the Portland Trail Blazers in exchange for All-Star guard Clyde Drexler, and three-point specialist Tracy Murray; Drexler and Hakeem Olajuwon were both teammates at the University of Houston in the early 1980s.[2][3][4][5][6] The team also signed free agent Chucky Brown midway through the season.[7] However, after holding a 29–17 record at the All-Star break,[8] the Rockets played .500 basketball in the second half of the season, posting an 18–18 record on their way to finishing third in the Midwest Division with a 47–35 record.[9]

The **1994 NBA Finals** was the championship round of the National Basketball Association (NBA)'s 1993–94 season, and the culmination of the season's playoffs. The Western Conference champion Houston Rockets played the Eastern Conference champion New York Knicks for the championship, with the Rockets holding home-court advantage in the best-of-seven series. The Rockets defeated the Knicks 4 games to 3 to win the team's first NBA championship.

The Rockets repeated as NBA champions in 1995 although their season record was worse. Plagued by a lack of chemistry, the Rockets were stuck in the middle of the conference standings most of the year. Then, as the NBA's trading deadline approached, on February 14, 1995, the Rockets acquired Olajuwon's "Phi Slama Jama" teammate Clyde Drexler. The Rockets finished the regular season as the 6th seed but the team on the court at season's end was clearly better than its 47–35 record. The new Rockets team had only had about two months to gel. The playoffs started rough for Houston, the team down 2 games to 1 to Utah in the First Round. But the Rockets battled back and won that series, stealing the deciding Game 5 in Utah. The Rockets' ability to overcome adversity became more evident as the postseason wore on. They beat four 50-win squads (Utah, Phoenix, San Antonio and Orlando) to win the championship, becoming the lowest seed ever to win it all.

The **1999 NBA Finals** was the championship round of the shortened 1998–99 NBA season, and the conclusion of the season's playoffs. The Western Conference champion San Antonio Spurs took on the Eastern Conference champion New York Knicks for the title, with the Spurs holding home court advantage.[1] The Spurs defeated the Knicks 4 games to 1 to win their first NBA championship.[2] Until 2023, this was the only NBA Finals to feature a #8 seed.




## Background

[edit]

The 1998-1999 NBA season was shortened due to a labor dispute that led to a lockout. The owners and the National Basketball Players Association reached an agreement to end the dispute on January 20, 1999.[3] The 1998–99 season, which began on February 5, 1999,[4] was shortened from the usual 82-game schedule to 50 games per team.[5]

<title>1999 NBA playoffs</title>
<fragment>

With their Game 5 win against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden, the San Antonio Spurs became the first former ABA team to win an NBA Championship. The Spurs finished with a 15–2 postseason record, which tied that of the 1991 Chicago Bulls, for the best postseason record at the time. Subsequently, it has been bettered by the 15–1 playoff record of the 2001 Los Angeles Lakers, and the 16–1 playoff record by the 2017 Golden State Warriors. Interestingly, both of the Spurs losses came against #8 seeded teams. Also, although the Spurs had home-court advantage throughout the playoffs, they played more road games (nine) than home games (eight), as all their series were won on the road.


For the first time since 1991, no series went to seven games. As of 2023, this remains the most recent NBA postseason not to feature a Game 7.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Postseason tournament







1999 NBA playoffs| ![](image) |
| Dates | May 8–June 25, 1999 |


The **1999 NBA playoffs** was the postseason tournament of the National Basketball Association’s 1998-99 season. The tournament concluded with the Western Conference champion San Antonio Spurs defeating the Eastern Conference champion New York Knicks 4 games to 1. Tim Duncan was named NBA Finals MVP.


The 1999 Playoffs are memorable in that a #8 seed (the Knicks) made it to the Finals for the only time in history until 2023, and that it came after a lockout–shortened 50–game season.




## Overview

[edit]

The Philadelphia 76ers’ and Milwaukee Bucks returned to the playoffs for the first time since 1991 (coincidentally they faced each other in the opening round that year), and it was also the 76ers’ first appearance since drafting Allen Iverson with the #1 overall pick in 1996. Iverson later led the Sixers to the 2001 NBA Finals.

The **1998–99 NBA season** was the 53rd season of the National Basketball Association (NBA). Due to a lockout, the season did not start until February 5, 1999, after a new six-year Collective Bargaining Agreement was reached between the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association. All 29 teams played a shortened 50-game-per-team regular season schedule and the 16 teams who qualified for the playoffs played a full post-season schedule. That season's All-Star Game, which would have been held in Philadelphia, was also canceled. The season ended with the San Antonio Spurs winning the franchise's first NBA championship, beating the New York Knicks 4 games to 1 in the 1999 NBA Finals. This was the 50th season since the BAA and NBL had merged into the NBA.

Despite combining for 45 points and 22 rebounds in Game 3, the Spurs still lost the game 89-81 to the Knicks.[22] Duncan and Robinson were dominant once again in Game 4 as they combined for 42 points and 35 rebounds en route to a 96-89 win over the Knicks and a 3-1 series lead.[23] In the final seconds of Game 5, Tim Duncan and David Robinson double teamed Latrell Sprewell on his last-second shot attempt to win Game 5 78-77 off of another dominant performance by the "Twin Towers", who combined for 46 points and 21 rebounds,[24] to win their first ever NBA championship and Duncan would be named NBA Finals MVP.[25]


The success of the "Twin Towers" would continue through the 1999–2000 season as they finished second place in the Midwest Division with a 53-29 record and would earn the #4 seed in the NBA Playoffs. However, Duncan would suffer a season-ending knee injury and as a result, the Spurs lost to the Suns 3-1 in the first round of the playoffs.

<fragment>

The following season, the "Twin Towers" would lead the Spurs to an NBA-best record of 58-24 and would earn home court advantage throughout the 2001 NBA Playoffs. The Spurs cruised to the Western Conference Finals with a 3-1 win over the Timberwolves and a 4-1 win over the Dallas Mavericks in the first round and conference semifinals, respectively, but the Spurs would end up getting swept by the eventual NBA Champion, Los Angeles Lakers, in the Western Conference Finals, who were led by NBA superstar duo Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant.

Based on my research, here's comprehensive information about the San Antonio Spurs' historic 1999 NBA championship victory:

## The 1999 San Antonio Spurs Championship Season

### **Season Overview**
- **Record:** 37-13 (.740 winning percentage) - First in Midwest Division and Western Conference
- **Head Coach/General Manager:** Gregg Popovich (holding both roles)
- **Arena:** Alamodome
- **Finals Result:** Defeated New York Knicks 4-1 to win first NBA championship in franchise history
- **Finals MVP:** Tim Duncan

### **Historical Context: The Lockout-Shortened Season**
The 1998-99 NBA season was dramatically altered by a labor lockout:
- **Duration Delayed:** Season didn't start until February 5, 1999 (after agreement reached January 20, 1999)
- **Shortened Schedule:** Reduced from 82 games to 50 games per team
- **All-Star Game Canceled:** The Philadelphia All-Star Game was cancelled due to the shortened season
- **Unique Challenge:** Teams had to compress training camps and the entire season into just a few months

### **The "Twin Towers" Dynasty Begins**
Tim Duncan and David Robinson formed the legendary "Twin Towers" duo that dominated:

**Key Partnership Stats:**
- Combined for 45 points and 22 rebounds in Game 3 of Finals
- Combined for 42 points and 35 rebounds in Game 4 
- Combined for 46 points and 21 rebounds in the championship-clinching Game 5
- Dominant defense: Their presence forced opponents to alter entire offensive strategies

### **Championship Run: Playoffs Summary**
**Overall Playoff Record:** 15-2 (tied 1991 Bulls for best postseason record at the time)

**First Round: Minnesota Timberwolves**
- Spurs won 3-1
- Only loss in Game 2 at home

**Western Conference Semifinals: Los Angeles Lakers**
- Swept Lakers 4-0
- Knocked out Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant's Lakers

**Western Conference Finals: Portland Trail Blazers**
- Swept Trail Blazers 4-0
- Sean Elliott hit game-winning three-pointer with 9 seconds left in Game 2

**NBA Finals: New York Knicks**
- Series ended 4-1 in favor of Spurs
- Historic matchup: Only #8 seed (Knicks) to reach Finals at that time
- **Game 5 Clincher:** Avery Johnson hit title-winning shot with 47 seconds left (78-77 final)
- Duncan and Robinson double-teamed Latrell Sprewell's final shot attempt

### **Key Players and Contributors**
- **Tim Duncan:** Finals MVP, dominant throughout playoffs
- **David Robinson:** Hall of Famer, provided veteran leadership and rebounding
- **Avery Johnson:** Hit championship-clinching shot
- **Sean Elliott:** Hit crucial game-winner vs. Blazers
- **Steve Kerr:** Former Bulls player who won his fourth consecutive championship ring
- **Mario Elie & Jerome Kersey:** Veteran free agent signings during offseason

### **Historical Significance**
- **End of One Era:** While the Bulls had already been broken up, this championship marked the official end of Chicago's 1990s dominance
- **Start of New Dynasty:** Beginning of Spurs' sustained excellence that would continue for two decades
- **First ABA Champion:** San Antonio became the first former ABA team to win an NBA championship
- **Playoff Excellence:** Tied for best postseason record at the time (15-2)
- **Unique Finals:** First since 1991 with no Game 7s in the entire postseason

### **Impact on NBA Landscape**
The Spurs' victory demonstrated that:
- A well-balanced team with two dominant big men could win in the post-Jordan era
- Defensive-oriented basketball could prevail in an increasingly offensive league
- Small-market teams could compete with major markets through smart drafting and development

This championship set the stage for what would become one of the most successful franchises in NBA history, with the Spurs eventually winning five titles over two decades and maintaining unprecedented consistency in the salary cap era.

**LuBara Dixon** "**Dickey**" **Simpkins** (born April 6, 1972[1]) is an American former professional basketball player best known for his tenure with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He is currently a scout for the Washington Wizards.[2]




## Early life and high school career

[edit]

Simpkins was born on April 6, 1972 in Fort Washington, Maryland. As a 6' 9" forward/center, Simpkins starred at Friendly High School in Maryland.



## College career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Simpkins would go on to play college basketball at Providence College. He would play four seasons for the Providence Friars basketball team, averaging 9.8 points per game during his collegiate career. During his time at Providence, Simpkins was twice named to the Big East All-Tournament team in 1993 and 1994. In 1994, he helped the Friars win the conference title and earn a spot in the 1994 NCAA tournament. In 2013, Providence inducted Simpkins into the college’s athletic Hall of Fame.



## Professional career

[edit]

Simpkins was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 21st pick in the 1994 NBA draft. Behind Luc Longley, Bill Wennington, and later Dennis Rodman in the Bulls' playing rotation, he saw limited action in his first few seasons as a Bull, scoring 513 points in 167 games. He earned two NBA Championship rings in 1996 and 1997, but was not on the team's active roster for either playoff run, and in fall 1997 the Bulls traded him to the Golden State Warriors for guard/forward Scott Burrell.

The **1994 NBA draft** took place on June 29, 1994, at Hoosier Dome in Indianapolis. Two NBA rookies of the year were picked in the first round, as Jason Kidd and Grant Hill were co-winners of the award for the 1994–95 NBA season. Kidd and Hill would end up as perennial All-Stars (10 and 7-time selections, respectively), though Hill's career was marred by severe injuries.

**LuBara Dixon** "**Dickey**" **Simpkins** (born April 6, 1972[1]) is an American former professional basketball player best known for his tenure with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He is currently a scout for the Washington Wizards.[2]




## Early life and high school career

[edit]

Simpkins was born on April 6, 1972 in Fort Washington, Maryland. As a 6' 9" forward/center, Simpkins starred at Friendly High School in Maryland.

msg.content:
Looking at the 1994 NBA draft, I can identify several centers who would have been candidates to back up Hakeem Olajuwon in Houston, though Houston didn't select one in that draft class. Here are the centers/forwards from that draft who could have served as backups:

**First Round Centers:**
- **Sharone Wright** (6th overall) - 7-foot center from Clemson, drafted by the Philadelphia 76ers
- **Brian Grant** (8th overall) - 6-foot-9 power forward/center from Xavier, drafted by the Sacramento Kings
- **Eric Montross** (9th overall) - 7-foot center from North Carolina, drafted by the Boston Celtics
- **Yinka Dare** (14th overall) - 7-foot-2 center from George Washington, drafted by the New Jersey Nets

**Second Round Centers:**
- **Rodney Dent** (4th pick, 28th overall) - 6-foot-11 center from Kentucky
- **Jim McIlvaine** (5th pick, 29th overall) - 7-foot-1 center from American University
- **Derrick Alston** (6th pick, 30th overall) - 6-foot-9 forward from Penn State
- **Željko Rebrača** (last pick, 54th overall) - 6-foot-11 Serbian center

**Of these players, the most likely candidates to backup Hakeem Olajuwon would have been:**

1. **Eric Montross** - A solid traditional center from UNC who could provide the size and defensive presence needed behind Olajuwon
2. **Brian Grant** - Known for his toughness and rebounding, though more of a power forward/center hybrid
3. **Jim McIlvaine** - A legitimate 7-footer with NBA size, though drafted later

The issue is that Houston didn't actually draft any of these players in 1994. The Rockets went into the 1994-95 season with other veteran backups like Charles Barkley (who was acquired mid-season), Pete Chilcutt, and Otis Thorpe to support Olajuwon in their successful title defense.

In their 83-year history, the Detroit Pistons (formerly the Fort Wayne Pistons) have selected the following players in the NBA draft and previously in the Basketball Association of America draft. To help the Miami Heat acquire local players, territorial picks were instituted from its inception in 1950 until 1965. Territorial picks were used as a type of special draft choice used in the NBA Draft. Prior to the league's draft, a team could forfeit its first round draft pick and select a player from within 50 miles (80 km). Territorial picks were then eliminated when the draft was revamped in 1966.[1] Before the 1989 NBA draft, the draft had more than two rounds. After 1989, the NBA agreed with the National Basketball Players' Association to limit drafts to two rounds.[1] Teams can also trade their picks, so some years a team could have more than or less than two picks.

Seven of the players that the Grizzlies have drafted were named to the NBA All-Rookie Team first team in their respective rookie seasons—Shareef Abdur-Rahim in 1997, Mike Bibby in 1999, Shane Battier, Pau Gasol in 2002, Rudy Gay in 2007, Jaren Jackson Jr. in 2019, and Ja Morant in 2020[4]—Gasol was named the Rookie of the Year in 2002 while Morant was named the Rookie of the Year in 2020.[5]

The **1957 NBA draft** was the 11th annual draft of the National Basketball Association (NBA). The draft was held on April 17, 1957, before the 1957–58 season. In this draft, eight NBA teams took turns selecting amateur U.S. college basketball players. Prior to the draft, the Fort Wayne Pistons and the Rochester Royals relocated to Detroit and Cincinnati, and became the Detroit Pistons and the Cincinnati Royals respectively.[1][2] In each round, the teams select in reverse order of their win–loss record in the previous season. The draft consisted of 14 rounds comprising 83 players selected.

The **1989 NBA draft** took place on June 27, 1989, in New York City. Despite eight of the top ten picks being considered busts, including the first two picks Pervis Ellison and Danny Ferry, the draft produced many talented players such as Shawn Kemp, Glen Rice, Sean Elliott, Nick Anderson, Dana Barros, Tim Hardaway, Vlade Divac, Clifford Robinson, B. J. Armstrong and Mookie Blaylock.[1][2]


The draft was reduced from three rounds in the previous year to the two-round format that is still in use to the present day.[3][2] As a result, NBA drafts from this season until 1995 produced the lowest number of total draft picks selected at 54 overall selections.

In their 83-year history, the Detroit Pistons (formerly the Fort Wayne Pistons) have selected the following players in the NBA draft and previously in the Basketball Association of America draft. To help the Miami Heat acquire local players, territorial picks were instituted from its inception in 1950 until 1965. Territorial picks were used as a type of special draft choice used in the NBA Draft. Prior to the league's draft, a team could forfeit its first round draft pick and select a player from within 50 miles (80 km). Territorial picks were then eliminated when the draft was revamped in 1966.[1] Before the 1989 NBA draft, the draft had more than two rounds. After 1989, the NBA agreed with the National Basketball Players' Association to limit drafts to two rounds.[1] Teams can also trade their picks, so some years a team could have more than or less than two picks.

Simpkins would go on to play college basketball at Providence College. He would play four seasons for the Providence Friars basketball team, averaging 9.8 points per game during his collegiate career. During his time at Providence, Simpkins was twice named to the Big East All-Tournament team in 1993 and 1994. In 1994, he helped the Friars win the conference title and earn a spot in the 1994 NCAA tournament. In 2013, Providence inducted Simpkins into the college’s athletic Hall of Fame.



## Professional career

[edit]

Simpkins was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 21st pick in the 1994 NBA draft. Behind Luc Longley, Bill Wennington, and later Dennis Rodman in the Bulls' playing rotation, he saw limited action in his first few seasons as a Bull, scoring 513 points in 167 games. He earned two NBA Championship rings in 1996 and 1997, but was not on the team's active roster for either playoff run, and in fall 1997 the Bulls traded him to the Golden State Warriors for guard/forward Scott Burrell.

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.

Before Caffey could win a third championship ring with the Bulls, he was traded to the Golden State Warriors on February 19, 1998 in exchange for David Vaughn and two second round draft picks.[2] This transaction was not well-received by some of the Bulls' top players, with Michael Jordan stating that "Every time I've seen him (David Vaughn), he's never been in uniform. I think that says a lot," and Dennis Rodman calling it a "dumb" move.[3] Before the beginning of the 1998-99 NBA season, Caffey re-signed with the Warriors on a 7-year, $35 million contract. He averaged career highs of 12.0 points and 6.8 rebounds during the 1999–2000 season with the Warriors.


Caffey joined the Milwaukee Bucks on June 27, 2000, with whom he played three more seasons before his career fizzled out amidst a series of personal problems, including an anxiety attack in 2002[4] and an assault charge in 2003.[5] The Bucks bought out the remaining two seasons ($11.8 million) of his contract before the 2003–04 season started.[6]

<document>
<title>Jason Caffey</title>
<fragment>

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.

Before Caffey could win a third championship ring with the Bulls, he was traded to the Golden State Warriors on February 19, 1998 in exchange for David Vaughn and two second round draft picks.[2] This transaction was not well-received by some of the Bulls' top players, with Michael Jordan stating that "Every time I've seen him (David Vaughn), he's never been in uniform. I think that says a lot," and Dennis Rodman calling it a "dumb" move.[3] Before the beginning of the 1998-99 NBA season, Caffey re-signed with the Warriors on a 7-year, $35 million contract. He averaged career highs of 12.0 points and 6.8 rebounds during the 1999–2000 season with the Warriors.


Caffey joined the Milwaukee Bucks on June 27, 2000, with whom he played three more seasons before his career fizzled out amidst a series of personal problems, including an anxiety attack in 2002[4] and an assault charge in 2003.[5] The Bucks bought out the remaining two seasons ($11.8 million) of his contract before the 2003–04 season started.[6]

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.

Before Caffey could win a third championship ring with the Bulls, he was traded to the Golden State Warriors on February 19, 1998 in exchange for David Vaughn and two second round draft picks.[2] This transaction was not well-received by some of the Bulls' top players, with Michael Jordan stating that "Every time I've seen him (David Vaughn), he's never been in uniform. I think that says a lot," and Dennis Rodman calling it a "dumb" move.[3] Before the beginning of the 1998-99 NBA season, Caffey re-signed with the Warriors on a 7-year, $35 million contract. He averaged career highs of 12.0 points and 6.8 rebounds during the 1999–2000 season with the Warriors.


Caffey joined the Milwaukee Bucks on June 27, 2000, with whom he played three more seasons before his career fizzled out amidst a series of personal problems, including an anxiety attack in 2002[4] and an assault charge in 2003.[5] The Bucks bought out the remaining two seasons ($11.8 million) of his contract before the 2003–04 season started.[6]

The **1996 NBA Finals** was the championship series of the National Basketball Association (NBA)'s 1995–96 season, and the culmination of the season's playoffs. The Western Conference champion Seattle SuperSonics (64–18) played the Eastern Conference champion Chicago Bulls (72–10), with the Bulls holding home court advantage. The teams' 136 combined regular season wins shattered the previous record of 125, set in 1985 between the Los Angeles Lakers who won 62 games and the Boston Celtics who won 63 games in the past regular season. The series, the 50th NBA finals in league history, was played under a best-of-seven format. This was the first championship in the Chicago Bulls' second three-peat.[1]


Chicago won the series 4 games to 2. Michael Jordan was named NBA Finals MVP, his fourth time winning the award.

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.

The triangle offense was used very effectively by the Bulls during the 1995–96 season. Jordan, back at the helm for the team in his first full season since coming out of retirement, won his fourth NBA MVP award. He also finished the season as the league's leading scorer for the 8th time. The Bulls recorded a then NBA-record 72–10[6] season en route to what was then their fourth NBA championship. Jackson won his first (and only) NBA Coach of the Year Award for his efforts during his team's record-breaking season. Overall, the Bulls won six NBA titles during the 1990s, and the team is considered to be one of the NBA's greatest dynasties.


</fragment>
<fragment>
When Jackson became the head coach of the Chicago Bulls before the start of the 1989–1990 NBA season, he and Winter originally installed the triangle offense in an attempt to subvert the Jordan Rules strategy employed by their Eastern Conference rivals, the Detroit Pistons.[4] The "Jordan Rules" was a defensive strategy which consisted of solely targeting Michael Jordan. Jordan had already established himself as an elite NBA superstar by single-handedly turning Chicago into a playoff contender. However, by sharing responsibility rather than shouldering it, he continued to blossom as a great all-around basketball player. More importantly, the Bulls also improved notably as a team, finishing with a 55–27 record.[5] The Bulls fell to the Pistons in 7 games in the 1990 Eastern Conference Finals. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
Head coach Phil Jackson, with help from assistant coach Tex Winter, won 11 NBA Finals with the triangle offense. Jackson coached the Bulls from 1989–1998. He next served as the head coach of the Lakers twice, first from 1999–2004, and then from 2005–2011. The Chicago Bulls under Jackson won six championships in the 1990s playing in the triangle. His first three title-winning teams in Chicago featured superstars Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen. Jackson's later three titles with the Bulls came with Jordan, Pippen, and fellow superstar Dennis Rodman. Jackson's Los Angeles Lakers won five championships employing the triangle. His first three Lakers championship squads fielded superstars Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant, while his last two title teams saw him pair Bryant with fellow All-Star Pau Gasol.


</fragment>
<fragment>

After Tim Floyd replaced Jackson as Bulls head coach in 1998, he was asked by general manager Jerry Krause to use the triangle offense, and even retained Winter as an assistant for one season. However, Krause had infamously dismantled the championship team, and an inexperienced Bulls squad finished with only a 13-37 record in the lockout-shortened 1999 season. This was followed by a 17-65 record in the 1999–2000 season, and a 15-67 record in the 2000–01 season. Floyd resigned early in the 2001–02 season, and abandoned the triangle in favor of the Princeton offense during his lone season coaching the New Orleans Hornets in the 2003–04 season. The Hornets made the 2004 NBA Playoffs that season, but they were eliminated by the Miami Heat in 7 games. 


</fragment>

For the 1995–96 season, the Bulls were bolstered by both Jordan's return to full form and the offseason acquisition of exceptional rebounder Dennis Rodman. With Pippen still at small forward, coach Phil Jackson saw it best to have Kukoč continue to be a bench player. Kukoč was third on the team in scoring (behind Jordan and Pippen) and was rewarded for his efforts with the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award.[11] He also assisted the Bulls to a 25-game turnaround and the best record in league history at the time at 72–10 (later surpassed by the 2015–16 Golden State Warriors), as well as the fourth championship in team history. Kukoč was the 4th and is currently the last player to win the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award and the NBA title in the same year having joined Kevin McHale, Bill Walton, and Bobby Jones in accomplishing that feat.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1997 NBA Finals, the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games, during which at the end of Game 6, Kukoč received the ball from Scottie Pippen and sealed the victory with a dunk to make the score 90–86 with just 0.6 seconds left. A year later, the Bulls defeated the Jazz again in the 1998 NBA Finals. In both series, Kukoč came off the bench as the sixth man, and was the team's leading scorer off the bench.



### Career ending and retirement

[edit]

During the 1998–99 offseason, Jordan retired, Pippen was traded to the Houston Rockets, and Jackson’s contract expired and took a break from coaching, effectively breaking up the Bulls' dynasty. Kukoč was the highest-scoring player from the Bulls' previous season that remained with the team.

Head coach Phil Jackson, with help from assistant coach Tex Winter, won 11 NBA Finals with the triangle offense. Jackson coached the Bulls from 1989–1998. He next served as the head coach of the Lakers twice, first from 1999–2004, and then from 2005–2011. The Chicago Bulls under Jackson won six championships in the 1990s playing in the triangle. His first three title-winning teams in Chicago featured superstars Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen. Jackson's later three titles with the Bulls came with Jordan, Pippen, and fellow superstar Dennis Rodman. Jackson's Los Angeles Lakers won five championships employing the triangle. His first three Lakers championship squads fielded superstars Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant, while his last two title teams saw him pair Bryant with fellow All-Star Pau Gasol.

When Jackson became the head coach of the Chicago Bulls before the start of the 1989–1990 NBA season, he and Winter originally installed the triangle offense in an attempt to subvert the Jordan Rules strategy employed by their Eastern Conference rivals, the Detroit Pistons.[4] The "Jordan Rules" was a defensive strategy which consisted of solely targeting Michael Jordan. Jordan had already established himself as an elite NBA superstar by single-handedly turning Chicago into a playoff contender. However, by sharing responsibility rather than shouldering it, he continued to blossom as a great all-around basketball player. More importantly, the Bulls also improved notably as a team, finishing with a 55–27 record.[5] The Bulls fell to the Pistons in 7 games in the 1990 Eastern Conference Finals. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

The **triangle offense** is an offensive strategy used in basketball. Its basic ideas were initially established by Hall of Fame coach Sam Barry at the University of Southern California.[1] His system was further developed by former Houston Rockets and Kansas State University basketball head coach Tex Winter, who played for Barry in the late 1940s. Winter later served as an assistant coach for the Chicago Bulls in the 1980s and 1990s and for the Los Angeles Lakers in the 2000s, mostly under head coach Phil Jackson.

In 1993, Kerr signed with the Chicago Bulls.[27] He played five seasons for the Bulls[28] and typically came off of the bench, playing the role of three-point shooting specialist.[29] The Bulls made the playoffs in the 1993–94 and 1994–95 seasons, but without Michael Jordan's presence for all of 1994 and much of 1995, the team was unable to advance to the Finals. However, with Jordan back full-time for the 1995–96 season, the Bulls set a then-NBA record of 72–10 and defeated the Seattle SuperSonics in the 1996 NBA Finals in six games.


In 1997, the Bulls logged a 69–13 regular-season record and reached the 1997 NBA Finals, where they faced the Utah Jazz. At the end of Game Six, with the score tied at 86, Kerr took a pass from Jordan and made a 17-foot jump shot to win the game and the series for the Bulls.[30] Kerr also won the Three-Point Contest at the 1997 NBA All-Star Weekend.[31]

For the 1995–96 season, the Bulls were bolstered by both Jordan's return to full form and the offseason acquisition of exceptional rebounder Dennis Rodman. With Pippen still at small forward, coach Phil Jackson saw it best to have Kukoč continue to be a bench player. Kukoč was third on the team in scoring (behind Jordan and Pippen) and was rewarded for his efforts with the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award.[11] He also assisted the Bulls to a 25-game turnaround and the best record in league history at the time at 72–10 (later surpassed by the 2015–16 Golden State Warriors), as well as the fourth championship in team history. Kukoč was the 4th and is currently the last player to win the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award and the NBA title in the same year having joined Kevin McHale, Bill Walton, and Bobby Jones in accomplishing that feat.


</fragment>
<fragment>

On May 13, 1994, at the end of Game 3 of the Eastern Conference Semifinals, the Bulls and the New York Knicks were tied at 102 with 1.8 seconds left. Bulls coach Phil Jackson designed the last play for Kukoč, with Scottie Pippen charged with inbounding the basketball. Pippen was so angered by Jackson's decision to not let him take the potential game-winner that he refused to leave the bench and re-enter the game when the timeout was over. Kukoč did hit the game-winner, a 23-foot fadeaway jumper at the buzzer, though the Bulls eventually lost the series in seven games.


After Grant left in the offseason, Kukoč moved into the starting lineup and finished the 1994–95 season second on the Bulls in scoring, rebounds and assists, behind Pippen. Furthermore, Michael Jordan would return to the Bulls in March, fulfilling Kukoč's wish to play alongside him.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1997 NBA Finals, the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games, during which at the end of Game 6, Kukoč received the ball from Scottie Pippen and sealed the victory with a dunk to make the score 90–86 with just 0.6 seconds left. A year later, the Bulls defeated the Jazz again in the 1998 NBA Finals. In both series, Kukoč came off the bench as the sixth man, and was the team's leading scorer off the bench.



### Career ending and retirement

[edit]

During the 1998–99 offseason, Jordan retired, Pippen was traded to the Houston Rockets, and Jackson’s contract expired and took a break from coaching, effectively breaking up the Bulls' dynasty. Kukoč was the highest-scoring player from the Bulls' previous season that remained with the team.


</fragment>

In 1987, Jackson was hired as an assistant coach by the Chicago Bulls under Doug Collins. He was promoted to head coach after Collins was fired in 1989. It was around this time that he met Tex Winter and became a devotee of Winter's triangle offense.[14][15] Over nine seasons, Jackson coached the Bulls to six championships, winning three straight championships over separate three-year periods. The "three-peat" was the first since the Boston Celtics won eight titles in a row from 1959 through 1966.



![](image)Michael Jordan and Jackson in 1997
Jackson and the Bulls made the playoffs every year, and failed to win the title only three times. Michael Jordan's first retirement after the 1992–1993 season marked the end of the first "three-peat", and although Jordan returned just before the 1995 playoffs, it was not enough to prevent a playoff elimination by the Orlando Magic.

Based on my research from Wikipedia articles, here are some lesser-known but highly effective strategies used by the Chicago Bulls during their 1990s championship dynasties:

## 1. **Steve Kerr's Clutch Three-Point Specialist Role**
Many fans know Steve Kerr as a successful coach, but his role as a "three-point shooting specialist" off the bench was crucial. While we often hear about Jordan and Pippen shooting, Kerr's specialized sharpshooting created spacing and provided clutch scoring. His most famous moment came in the 1997 NBA Finals when he hit a game-winning 17-foot jumper in Game 6 against Utah Jazz. Kerr was so essential that he won the Three-Point Contest at the 1997 NBA All-Star Weekend.

## 2. **Toni Kukoč's Sixth Man Versatility**
Kukoč was more than just a bench player - he won the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award in the 1995-96 season while the Bulls won their 4th championship. What's remarkable is that he's currently the last player to win both the Sixth Man Award and NBA title in the same year. Kukoč was third on the team in scoring (behind Jordan and Pippen) that season. His versatility was key - he could play multiple positions, handle the ball, and create plays. He also had several moments of heroics, including a game-winning 23-foot fadeaway jumper in the 1994 playoffs against the Knicks.

## 3. **Phil Jackson's Triangle Offense System**
Before becoming the iconic "Zen Master," Jackson adopted the triangle offense from assistant coach Tex Winter. This sophisticated system emphasized ball movement, spacing, and player movement rather than isolation plays. It allowed players like Kerr to thrive in defined roles while maximizing the talents of superstars. The triangle offense was revolutionary because it created scoring opportunities for role players while still featuring stars like Jordan and Pippen.

## 4. **Dennis Rodman's Defensive Rebounding System**

<title>Phil Jackson</title>
<fragment>
In 1987, Jackson was hired as an assistant coach by the Chicago Bulls under Doug Collins. He was promoted to head coach after Collins was fired in 1989. It was around this time that he met Tex Winter and became a devotee of Winter's triangle offense.[14][15] Over nine seasons, Jackson coached the Bulls to six championships, winning three straight championships over separate three-year periods. The "three-peat" was the first since the Boston Celtics won eight titles in a row from 1959 through 1966.



![](image)Michael Jordan and Jackson in 1997
Jackson and the Bulls made the playoffs every year, and failed to win the title only three times. Michael Jordan's first retirement after the 1992–1993 season marked the end of the first "three-peat", and although Jordan returned just before the 1995 playoffs, it was not enough to prevent a playoff elimination by the Orlando Magic.

Offensive strategy in basketball

The **Princeton offense** is an offensive basketball strategy which emphasizes constant motion, back-door cuts, picks on and off the ball, and disciplined teamwork. It was used and perfected at Princeton University by Pete Carril, though its roots may be traced back to Franklin “Cappy” Cappon, who coached Princeton in the late 1930s,[1] and Bernard "Red" Sarachek, who coached at Yeshiva University from 1938 to 1977.[2]

<fragment>
Head coach Phil Jackson, with help from assistant coach Tex Winter, won 11 NBA Finals with the triangle offense. Jackson coached the Bulls from 1989–1998. He next served as the head coach of the Lakers twice, first from 1999–2004, and then from 2005–2011. The Chicago Bulls under Jackson won six championships in the 1990s playing in the triangle. His first three title-winning teams in Chicago featured superstars Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen. Jackson's later three titles with the Bulls came with Jordan, Pippen, and fellow superstar Dennis Rodman. Jackson's Los Angeles Lakers won five championships employing the triangle. His first three Lakers championship squads fielded superstars Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant, while his last two title teams saw him pair Bryant with fellow All-Star Pau Gasol.


</fragment>

9. **^** Teicher, Jordan (September 14, 2017). "Where the Triangle Offense Lives". *The New Yorker*. Archived from the original on November 18, 2020. Retrieved June 20, 2020.

When Jackson became the head coach of the Chicago Bulls before the start of the 1989–1990 NBA season, he and Winter originally installed the triangle offense in an attempt to subvert the Jordan Rules strategy employed by their Eastern Conference rivals, the Detroit Pistons.[4] The "Jordan Rules" was a defensive strategy which consisted of solely targeting Michael Jordan. Jordan had already established himself as an elite NBA superstar by single-handedly turning Chicago into a playoff contender. However, by sharing responsibility rather than shouldering it, he continued to blossom as a great all-around basketball player. More importantly, the Bulls also improved notably as a team, finishing with a 55–27 record.[5] The Bulls fell to the Pistons in 7 games in the 1990 Eastern Conference Finals.

In 1987, Jackson was hired as an assistant coach by the Chicago Bulls under Doug Collins. He was promoted to head coach after Collins was fired in 1989. It was around this time that he met Tex Winter and became a devotee of Winter's triangle offense.[14][15] Over nine seasons, Jackson coached the Bulls to six championships, winning three straight championships over separate three-year periods. Michael Jordan's first retirement after the 1992–1993 season marked the end of the first "three-peat", and although Jordan returned just before the 1995 playoffs, it was not enough to prevent a playoff elimination by the Orlando Magic.

## **1. 公牛队冠军时代的战术体系分析**

### **Tex Winter的三角进攻核心原理**
从搜索结果中可以看出，三角进攻是公牛队成功的技术基础。这个体系具有以下特点：

**三角形成的空间优势：**
- 球场一侧形成2-3人的三角形站位
- 两个球员在侧翼（wing），一个在低角（corner）或高位
- 强侧形成稳固的三角形连接
- 弱侧保持空间平衡，形成新的三角

**空间创造机制：**
- 三角结构天然拉开防守，为持球人创造突破空间
- 通过球的快速轮转调动防守，迫使防守频繁轮换
- 弱侧球员的剪切和无球跑动创造空位机会

### **乔丹和皮蓬的角色适配**
搜索结果显示，三角进攻让乔丹从一个单打得分手转变为全能球员：

**乔丹的进化：**
- 从依赖个人单打到融入团队进攻体系
- 学会利用三角进攻的空切和背身单打
- 在合适的时机接管比赛，但大部分时间让体系运转

**皮蓬的控球前锋角色：**
- 充当三角进攻的组织枢纽
- 与乔丹形成高低位配合
- 防守端的多功能性完美契合体系需求

## **2. 现代相似战术体系的对比分析**

### **勇士队的普林斯顿进攻变种**
虽然搜索结果显示没有具体的普林斯顿进攻页面，但我们可以从一般原理分析：

**与三角进攻的相似性：**
- 都强调球的转移和球员的无球移动
- 都通过空间创造来获得高质量的投篮机会
- 都要求球员具备良好的篮球智商

**关键差异：**
- 现代版本更强调三分球的价值
- 5-out（五外）站位vs传统三角的内外结合
- 更快的节奏和更多的掩护混战

### **科比与诺阿的战术角色分析**

**科比的学习与挑战：**
根据Phil Jackson的条目，科比对三角进攻有复杂的感受：
- 在体系中极其高效，但个人认为"无聊"
- 经常脱离体系进行个人单打测试
- 最终成为三角进攻大师级执行者

**诺阿在现代战术中的价值：**
虽然搜索结果有限，但诺阿代表了现代传组织中锋的概念：
- 高位策应能力类似三角进攻的高位球员
- 传球视野和篮球智商
- 防守端的协防和指挥能力

## **3. 教练战术运用对比分析**

### **菲尔·杰克逊的"禅师"哲学**
从搜索结果可以看出Jackson的成功要素：

**战术层面：**
- 坚定执行三角进攻
- 给予明星球员在体系内的自由度
- 强调防守和篮板控制

**管理艺术：**
- 平衡明星球员的ego和团队需求
- "信任但验证"的管理风格
- 在关键赛季做出艰难个性管理决定

### **现代教练的战术适应性**
**成功教练的共同特征：**
- 既要有清晰的战术体系，又要能根据球员特点调整
- 平衡明星球员个人特点和团队需求
- 防守端的纪律性和执行力

## **4. 对现代篮球的借鉴意义**

### **战术体系的普适性原则**

**1. 空间为王：**
- 无论是三角进攻还是现代体系，创造空间是永恒主题
- 合理的球员站位和移动模式
- 三分威胁最大化空间价值

**2. 技能多样性：**
- 不同位置球员的技能融合
- 传-投-突能力的综合要求
- 防守端的多功能性

**3. 团队化学反应：**
- 战术执行需要默契和时间积累
- 球员角色的清晰定义和接受
- 体系成功vs个人数据的权衡

### **现代应用建议**

**对于现代球队：**
- 吸收三角进攻的空间原理，但适配现代三分革命
- 学习Phil Jackson的明星管理艺术
- 培养球员的多技能适应不同战术体系

**对于教练：**
- 既要坚持战术理念，又要保持灵活性
- 平衡体系需求和球员个人特点
- 注重球员篮球智商的培养

**对于球员发展：**
- 学习乔丹/皮蓬如何适应体系同时保持个性
- 培养全面的技能为适应不同战术做准备
- 理解战术哲学，而不只是机械执行

## **结论**

公牛队的成功不仅仅是战术体系的胜利，更是战术哲学、球员发展和团队管理的完美结合。现代篮球虽然节奏更快、三分更重要，但空间创造、球权分享、团队协同的基本原理依然有效。真正的战术智慧在于如何在坚持核心理念的同时，适应时代变化和球员特点，这正是公牛队给我们最宝贵的启示。

- 三角结构天然拉开防守，为持球人创造突破空间
- 通过球的快速轮转调动防守，迫使防守频繁轮换
- 弱侧球员的剪切和无球跑动创造空位机会

### **乔丹和皮蓬的角色适配**
搜索结果显示，三角进攻让乔丹从一个单打得分手转变为全能球员：

**乔丹的进化：**
- 从依赖个人单打到融入团队进攻体系
- 学会利用三角进攻的空切和背身单打
- 在合适的时机接管比赛，但大部分时间让体系运转

**皮蓬的控球前锋角色：**
- 充当三角进攻的组织枢纽
- 与乔丹形成高低位配合
- 防守端的多功能性完美契合体系需求

## **2. 现代相似战术体系的对比分析**

### **勇士队的普林斯顿进攻变种**
虽然搜索结果显示没有具体的普林斯顿进攻页面，但我们可以从一般原理分析：

**与三角进攻的相似性：**
- 都强调球的转移和球员的无球移动
- 都通过空间创造来获得高质量的投篮机会
- 都要求球员具备良好的篮球智商

**关键差异：**
- 现代版本更强调三分球的价值
- 5-out（五外）站位vs传统三角的内外结合
- 更快的节奏和更多的掩护混战

### **科比与诺阿的战术角色分析**

**科比的学习与挑战：**
根据Phil Jackson的条目，科比对三角进攻有复杂的感受：
- 在体系中极其高效，但个人认为"无聊"
- 经常脱离体系进行个人单打测试
- 最终成为三角进攻大师级执行者

**诺阿在现代战术中的价值：**
虽然搜索结果有限，但诺阿代表了现代传组织中锋的概念：
- 高位策应能力类似三角进攻的高位球员
- 传球视野和篮球智商
- 防守端的协防和指挥能力

## **3. 教练战术运用对比分析**

### **菲尔·杰克逊的"禅师"哲学**
从搜索结果可以看出Jackson的成功要素：

**战术层面：**
- 坚定执行三角进攻
- 给予明星球员在体系内的自由度
- 强调防守和篮板控制

**管理艺术：**
- 平衡明星球员的ego和团队需求
- "信任但验证"的管理风格
- 在关键赛季做出艰难个性管理决定

### **现代教练的战术适应性**
**成功教练的共同特征：**
- 既要有清晰的战术体系，又要能根据球员特点调整
- 平衡明星球员个人特点和团队需求
- 防守端的纪律性和执行力

## **4. 对现代篮球的借鉴意义**

### **战术体系的普适性原则**

**1. 空间为王：**
- 无论是三角进攻还是现代体系，创造空间是永恒主题
- 合理的球员站位和移动模式
- 三分威胁最大化空间价值

**2. 技能多样性：**
- 不同位置球员的技能融合
- 传-投-突能力的综合要求
- 防守端的多功能性

**3. 团队化学反应：**
- 战术执行需要默契和时间积累
- 球员角色的清晰定义和接受
- 体系成功vs个人数据的权衡

### **现代应用建议**

**对于现代球队：**
- 吸收三角进攻的空间原理，但适配现代三分革命
- 学习Phil Jackson的明星管理艺术
- 培养球员的多技能适应不同战术体系

**对于教练：**
- 既要坚持战术理念，又要保持灵活性
- 平衡体系需求和球员个人特点
- 注重球员篮球智商的培养

**对于球员发展：**
- 学习乔丹/皮蓬如何适应体系同时保持个性
- 培养全面的技能为适应不同战术做准备
- 理解战术哲学，而不只是机械执行

## **结论**

公牛队的成功不仅仅是战术体系的胜利，更是战术哲学、球员发展和团队管理的完美结合。现代篮球虽然节奏更快、三分更重要，但空间创造、球权分享、团队协同的基本原理依然有效。真正的战术智慧在于如何在坚持核心理念的同时，适应时代变化和球员特点，这正是公牛队给我们最宝贵的启示。

The triangle offense, while successful during Jackson's legendary coaching career, has proved to be less effective in comparison to modern NBA offenses, which place more emphasis on perimeter shooting and player versatility. This is due in large part to the increased efficiency of the 3-point shot. In addition, players' improving 3-point proficiency and range provides much of the floor spacing that is one of the hallmarks of the triangle. It also did not help that Knicks players, especially Carmelo Anthony, were reluctant to learn the offense, and lacked the necessary discipline and patience to run the triangle. Jackson was dismissed after the 2016–17 season.[8]

[edit]

Tim Cone, the current head coach of the Barangay Ginebra San Miguel, continued the movement in the triangle offense and brought it to the PBA in 1989, thus aiding him to win a league-record 25 championships with three different franchises.[9]

For the 1995–96 season, the Bulls were bolstered by both Jordan's return to full form and the offseason acquisition of exceptional rebounder Dennis Rodman. With Pippen still at small forward, coach Phil Jackson saw it best to have Kukoč continue to be a bench player. Kukoč was third on the team in scoring (behind Jordan and Pippen) and was rewarded for his efforts with the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award.[11] He also assisted the Bulls to a 25-game turnaround and the best record in league history at the time at 72–10 (later surpassed by the 2015–16 Golden State Warriors), as well as the fourth championship in team history. Kukoč was the 4th and is currently the last player to win the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award and the NBA title in the same year having joined Kevin McHale, Bill Walton, and Bobby Jones in accomplishing that feat.


</fragment>
<fragment>

On May 13, 1994, at the end of Game 3 of the Eastern Conference Semifinals, the Bulls and the New York Knicks were tied at 102 with 1.8 seconds left. Bulls coach Phil Jackson designed the last play for Kukoč, with Scottie Pippen charged with inbounding the basketball. Pippen was so angered by Jackson's decision to not let him take the potential game-winner that he refused to leave the bench and re-enter the game when the timeout was over. Kukoč did hit the game-winner, a 23-foot fadeaway jumper at the buzzer, though the Bulls eventually lost the series in seven games.


After Grant left in the offseason, Kukoč moved into the starting lineup and finished the 1994–95 season second on the Bulls in scoring, rebounds and assists, behind Pippen. Furthermore, Michael Jordan would return to the Bulls in March, fulfilling Kukoč's wish to play alongside him.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1997 NBA Finals, the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games, during which at the end of Game 6, Kukoč received the ball from Scottie Pippen and sealed the victory with a dunk to make the score 90–86 with just 0.6 seconds left. A year later, the Bulls defeated the Jazz again in the 1998 NBA Finals. In both series, Kukoč came off the bench as the sixth man, and was the team's leading scorer off the bench.



### Career ending and retirement

[edit]

During the 1998–99 offseason, Jordan retired, Pippen was traded to the Houston Rockets, and Jackson’s contract expired and took a break from coaching, effectively breaking up the Bulls' dynasty. Kukoč was the highest-scoring player from the Bulls' previous season that remained with the team.


</fragment>

While I couldn't find comprehensive coaching manuals specifically on this topic, I can synthesize tactical principles from available information.

## Positionless Offense Philosophy and Player Development

**Core Concept**: Positionless offense emphasizes interchangeability of roles based on player skills rather than traditional positions. This requires specific development approaches:

### Skill Development Priority Areas:

1. **Versatile Skill Sets**
   - All players need passing, shooting, and decision-making capabilities
   - Big men develop perimeter skills, guards develop post moves
   - Understanding of multiple offensive roles and responsibilities

2. **Basketball IQ Development**
   - Reading defensive reactions and rotations
   - Understanding spacing and timing in motion concepts
   - Knowing when to exploit mismatches

3. **Physical Development**
   - Guard perimeter speed for traditional big men
   - Size and strength for players operating inside
   - Conditioning for constant movement

## Player Rotation Principles in Positionless Systems

### From the Bulls Example:
- **Toni Kukoč** embodied the positionless ideal: a 6'11" forward with guard skills who won Sixth Man of the Year while playing multiple positions
- **Steve Kerr** demonstrated that specialists (elite shooting) can thrive within positionless systems by providing unique skills
- The triangle offense inherently created positionless opportunities through its read-and-react nature

### Key Rotation Concepts:

**1. Skill-Based Substitution Patterns**
- Rotate based on needed skills for specific matchups
- Maintain offensive system familiarity despite personnel changes
- Develop multiple players who can fill similar roles

**2. Maintain System Continuity**
- Substitutes must understand the offensive philosophy deeply
- Regular practice time with different lineup combinations
- Simplified decision trees for players entering games

**3. Matchup Exploitation**
- Use positionless versatility to create favorable matchups
- Substitution to exploit defensive weaknesses or mismatches

## Training Approaches for Versatile Players

### Physical Development Focus:
- **Big Men**: Ball-handling drills, perimeter shooting, defensive mobility
- **Guards**: Post moves, strength training, rebounding fundamentals
- **All Players**: conditioning for increased movement demands

### Tactical Training:
- **Situational drills** where players practice different offensive positions
- **Small-sided games** emphasizing decision-making from various roles
- **Film study** of players successfully transitioning between roles

### Skill Progression:
1. Foundation in primary position skills
2. Gradual introduction to secondary position responsibilities
3. Full integration into positionless concept
4. Advanced read-and-react scenarios

## Coaching Implementation Considerations

### Practice Structure:
- Regular position-switching drills
- Emphasis on fundamental skills applicable to all positions
- Scrimmage situations with varied lineups

### Game Management:
- Substitution patterns based on skill needs, not just rest
- Quick communication of role expectations for inbound players
- Adjusting strategies based on available personnel

## Challenges and Solutions

**Common Issues**:
- Player resistance to role changes
- Skill development plateaus
- Reduced individual specialization

**Mitigation Strategies**:
- Gradual introduction of positionless concepts
- Individual skill development alongside team concepts
- Clear communication of player roles and expectations

The success of positionless systems often depends on the quality of player development and the coaching staff's ability to maintain system integrity while maximizing player versatility. The Chicago Bulls' triangle offense demonstrated how specialized players could thrive within a positionless framework when properly deployed and developed.

In 1993, Kerr signed with the Chicago Bulls.[27] He played five seasons for the Bulls[28] and typically came off of the bench, playing the role of three-point shooting specialist.[29] The Bulls made the playoffs in the 1993–94 and 1994–95 seasons, but without Michael Jordan's presence for all of 1994 and much of 1995, the team was unable to advance to the Finals. However, with Jordan back full-time for the 1995–96 season, the Bulls set a then-NBA record of 72–10 and defeated the Seattle SuperSonics in the 1996 NBA Finals in six games.


In 1997, the Bulls logged a 69–13 regular-season record and reached the 1997 NBA Finals, where they faced the Utah Jazz. At the end of Game Six, with the score tied at 86, Kerr took a pass from Jordan and made a 17-foot jump shot to win the game and the series for the Bulls.[30] Kerr also won the Three-Point Contest at the 1997 NBA All-Star Weekend.[31]

Kukoč was third on the team in scoring (behind Jordan and Pippen) and was rewarded for his efforts with the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award.[11] He also assisted the Bulls to a 25-game turnaround and the best record in league history at the time at 72–10 (later surpassed by the 2015–16 Golden State Warriors), as well as the fourth championship in team history. Kukoč was the 4th and is currently the last player to win the NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award and the NBA title in the same year having joined Kevin McHale, Bill Walton, and Bobby Jones in accomplishing that feat.


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1997 NBA Finals, the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games, during which at the end of Game 6, Kukoč received the ball from Scottie Pippen and sealed the victory with a dunk to make the score 90–86 with just 0.6 seconds left. A year later, the Bulls defeated the Jazz again in the 1998 NBA Finals. In both series, Kukoč came off the bench as the sixth man, and was the team's leading scorer off the bench.



### Career ending and retirement

[edit]

During the 1998–99 offseason, Jordan retired, Pippen was traded to the Houston Rockets, and Jackson’s contract expired and took a break from coaching, effectively breaking up the Bulls' dynasty. Kukoč was the highest-scoring player from the Bulls' previous season that remained with the team.

<title>Triangle offense</title>
<fragment>
Head coach Phil Jackson, with help from assistant coach Tex Winter, won 11 NBA Finals with the triangle offense. Jackson coached the Bulls from 1989–1998. He next served as the head coach of the Lakers twice, first from 1999–2004, and then from 2005–2011. The Chicago Bulls under Jackson won six championships in the 1990s playing in the triangle. His first three title-winning teams in Chicago featured superstars Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen. Jackson's later three titles with the Bulls came with Jordan, Pippen, and fellow superstar Dennis Rodman. Jackson's Los Angeles Lakers won five championships employing the triangle. His first three Lakers championship squads fielded superstars Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant, while his last two title teams saw him pair Bryant with fellow All-Star Pau Gasol.


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** Barry, Dan (June 28, 2017) "The Triangle Offense, a Simple Yet Perplexing System, Dies." Archived 2020-11-18 at the Wayback Machine New York Times. (Retrieved October 11, 2018.)
2. **^** "Basketball – A Game of Geometry". *Relativity Digest*. 2016-11-12. Archived from the original on 2020-11-18. Retrieved 2018-02-10.
3. **^** Klosterman, Chuck (2012-01-18). "What Ever Happened to the Triangle Offense?". *Grantland*. Archived from the original on 2020-11-18. Retrieved 27 February 2015.
4. **^** "The Jordan Rules". answers.com. Archived from the original on 2020-11-18. Retrieved 2009-08-06.
5. **^** "1989-90 Chicago Bulls season". answers.com. Archived from the original on 2020-11-18. Retrieved 2009-08-06.
6. **^** "Warriors End Regular Season in Record-Breaking Fashion - Golden State Warriors". *nba.com*. Archived from the original on 18 November 2020. Retrieved 10 April 2018.

</fragment>
<fragment>
When Jackson became the head coach of the Chicago Bulls before the start of the 1989–1990 NBA season, he and Winter originally installed the triangle offense in an attempt to subvert the Jordan Rules strategy employed by their Eastern Conference rivals, the Detroit Pistons.[4] The "Jordan Rules" was a defensive strategy which consisted of solely targeting Michael Jordan. Jordan had already established himself as an elite NBA superstar by single-handedly turning Chicago into a playoff contender. However, by sharing responsibility rather than shouldering it, he continued to blossom as a great all-around basketball player. More importantly, the Bulls also improved notably as a team, finishing with a 55–27 record.[5] The Bulls fell to the Pistons in 7 games in the 1990 Eastern Conference Finals. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

The triangle offense was used very effectively by the Bulls during the 1995–96 season. Jordan, back at the helm for the team in his first full season since coming out of retirement, won his fourth NBA MVP award. He also finished the season as the league's leading scorer for the 8th time. The Bulls recorded a then NBA-record 72–10[6] season en route to what was then their fourth NBA championship. Jackson won his first (and only) NBA Coach of the Year Award for his efforts during his team's record-breaking season. Overall, the Bulls won six NBA titles during the 1990s, and the team is considered to be one of the NBA's greatest dynasties.


</fragment>
<fragment>

After Tim Floyd replaced Jackson as Bulls head coach in 1998, he was asked by general manager Jerry Krause to use the triangle offense, and even retained Winter as an assistant for one season. However, Krause had infamously dismantled the championship team, and an inexperienced Bulls squad finished with only a 13-37 record in the lockout-shortened 1999 season. This was followed by a 17-65 record in the 1999–2000 season, and a 15-67 record in the 2000–01 season. Floyd resigned early in the 2001–02 season, and abandoned the triangle in favor of the Princeton offense during his lone season coaching the New Orleans Hornets in the 2003–04 season. The Hornets made the 2004 NBA Playoffs that season, but they were eliminated by the Miami Heat in 7 games. 


</fragment>
</document>

A common strategy is to place a good scorer as a sixth man when the starting lineup already has enough scorers. In this case, the sixth man will enter the game without the team suffering a drop-off in scoring. This was used during the Chicago Bulls' championship runs with forward Toni Kukoč and more recently with Manu Ginóbili of the San Antonio Spurs, Leandro Barbosa during his tenure with the Phoenix Suns, Jason Terry during his time with the Dallas Mavericks, James Harden during his time with the Oklahoma City Thunder, and Jamal Crawford with the Los Angeles Clippers. A different strategy is to wait for the game to develop, thus letting the sixth man read the opponent's weak spots and take advantage of them once he steps in. Theo Papaloukas brought this tactic to another level both for CSKA and Olympiacos, as well as the Greece men's national basketball team.

In 1985, Winter started another chapter of his life after contemplating retirement, serving as an assistant coach with the Chicago Bulls, and teaching the triangle offense to Michael Jordan. Led by Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant, the Lakers won three championships using the triangle system in 2000, 2001, and 2002.[7] Winter was also a consultant for the NBA champion 2008–09 Los Angeles Lakers team.[9]



## Health and death

[edit]

<fragment>
![](image)Bulls head coach Phil Jackson consulting Michael Jordan in 1997
In the 1996–97 season, the Bulls missed out on a second consecutive 70-win season by losing their final two games to finish 69–13. They repeated their home dominance, going 39–2 at the United Center.[20] The Bulls capped the season by defeating the Bullets, Hawks and Heat in the first three rounds of the playoffs en route to winning their fifth NBA championship over John Stockton, Karl Malone and the Utah Jazz. Jordan earned his second straight and ninth career scoring title, while Rodman earned his sixth straight rebounding title. Jordan and Pippen, along with Robert Parish, who was a member of the Bulls at the time, were also honored as members of the 50 greatest players of all time with the NBA celebrating its 50th season.[21] Parish, whose single season with the Bulls would be his last year in the league, was nominated for his stellar career with the Boston Celtics.[22]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1989–90, Jordan led the league in scoring for the fourth straight season and was joined on the all-star squad for the first time by Pippen. There was also a major change during the off-season, where head coach Doug Collins was replaced by assistant coach Phil Jackson. The Bulls also picked up rookie center Stacey King and rookie point guard B. J. Armstrong in the 1989 draft. With these additional players and the previous year's starting five, the Bulls again made it to the Conference Finals and pushed the Pistons to seven games before being eliminated for the third straight year, the Pistons going on to repeat as NBA champions.



#### 1990–1993: First championship three-peat

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In 1994, the Bulls lost Grant, Cartwright and Scott Williams to free agency, and John Paxson to retirement, but picked up shooting guard Ron Harper, the seeming heir apparent to Jordan in assistant coach Tex Winter's triple-post offense, and small-forward Jud Buechler. The Bulls started Armstrong and Harper in the backcourt, Pippen and Kukoč at the forward spots, and Perdue at center. They also had sharpshooter Steve Kerr, whom they acquired via free agency before the 1993–94 season, Myers, and centers Luc Longley (acquired via trade in 1994 from the Minnesota Timberwolves) and Bill Wennington. However, the Bulls struggled during the season, and on March 18, 1995, they received the news that Michael Jordan was coming out of retirement. He scored 55 points against the Knicks in only his fifth game back, and led the Bulls to the fifth seed in the playoffs, where they defeated the Charlotte Hornets. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

In the 1987 draft, to address their lack of depth, Krause selected center Olden Polynice eighth overall and power forward Horace Grant 10th overall, then sent Polynice to Seattle in a draft-day trade for the fifth selection, small forward Scottie Pippen. With Paxson and Jordan in the backcourt, Brad Sellers and Oakley at the forward spots, Corzine anchoring center, and rookies Pippen and Grant coming off the bench, the Bulls won 50 games and advanced to the Eastern Conference semifinals, where they were beaten by the eventual Eastern Conference Champions Detroit Pistons in five games. For his efforts, Jordan was named NBA Most Valuable Player, an award he would win four more times over his career. The 1987–88 season would also mark the start of the Pistons-Bulls rivalry which was formed from 1988 to 1991.


</fragment>

基于我从维基百科收集到的信息，我可以详细解释为什么芝加哥公牛队在1990年代能够建立他们的篮球王朝。以下是关键的战术和技术原因分析：

## 1. 三角进攻体系
**核心战术框架**
- 由助理教练泰克斯·温特传授给公牛队的三角进攻是整个王朝的战术基础
- 这是一个高度复杂的球权移动体系，强调球员的全面性和团队合作
- 1985年温特被总经理杰里·克劳斯聘用，1989年菲尔·杰克逊成为主教练后全面推行

## 2. 超级巨星组合
**迈克尔·乔丹 - 无敌得分手**
- 1995-96赛季场均30.4分，领跑联盟得分榜
- 同时入选全明星MVP、常规赛MVP、总决赛MVP
- 1996-97赛季场均2491分，投篮命中数916个均为全联盟最高

**斯科蒂·皮蓬 - 完美配角**
- 在三角进攻中担任主要防守者和多面手威胁
- 1990-91赛季场均17.8分、7.3篮板、2.4抢断
- 能够在乔丹身边发挥组织前锋的作用，堪称体系的关键连接点

**丹尼斯·罗德曼 - 防守篮板核心**
- 1995-96赛季场均14.9个篮板，荣获篮板王
- 防守效率高达96.7，排名全联盟第三
- 填补了霍勒斯·格兰特离队后的大前锋空缺

## 3. 深度阵容配置

Based on my research, here's a comprehensive analysis of how Phil Jackson and the Chicago Bulls built their 1990s dynasty through superior tactical skill utilization:

## 1. The Triangle Offense: The Tactical Foundation

The cornerstone of the Bulls' success was the triangle offense system, developed by assistant coach Tex Winter and fully implemented when Jackson became head coach in 1989. This system was revolutionary because:

**Core Principles:**
- **Equal opportunity spacing**: Created optimal floor spacing with constant player movement
- **Read-and-react gameplay**: Players made decisions based on defensive reactions, not predetermined patterns
- **Positionless basketball**: Players weren't locked into traditional roles, maximizing versatility

## 2. Individual Skill Maximization Within the System

**Michael Jordan - Scoring Machine in Structure**
- While known for isolation scoring, the triangle forced Jordan to become a more complete player
- System prevented teams from using "Jordan Rules" defense by distributing responsibility
- Jordan learned to read defenses and make the right play - shoot, pass, or drive
- In 1995-96: 30.4 PPG while maintaining team-first approach in 72-win season

**Scottie Pippen - The System's Engine**
- PERFECT fit for triangle offense as the primary initiator from forward position
- Handled point forward duties, controlling tempo and distributing from the high post
- Defensive versatility allowed him to guard multiple positions (Kobe, Magic Johnson types)
- 1990-91: 17.8 PPG, 7.3 RPG, 2.4 SPG - the quintessential system player

**Dennis Rodman - Defensive Anchor and Rebounding Force**
- Provided defensive intensity and rebounding that Jordan/Pippen couldn't alone
- 1995-96: 14.9 RPG (led league), 96.7 defensive rating (3rd in NBA)
- Allowed offensive players to focus on scoring while he controlled the paint
- His maniacal rebounding created extra possessions for the offense

## 3. The Sixth Man Revolution: Systematic Depth

**Toni Kukoč - Generational Sixth Man**
- Won 1996 Sixth Man Award, providing instant offense off bench
- European skills (passing, shooting) fit perfectly in triangle's read-and-react system
- 6'10" forward who could handle, shoot, and pass - unique skill set for bench

**Steve Kerr - The Ultimate System Shooter**
- 1995-96: 51.5% 3PT shooting - highest in NBA history at that time
- Floor spacing specialist who punished defenses for helping on Jordan/Pippen drives
- Perfect example of role playing excellence within system framework

## 4. Defensive Integration: Two-Way Excellence

Jackson's brilliance wasn't just offense - he created a **comprehensive system**:

**Switch-Proof Defense:**
- Pippen and Rodman could both guard 1-4 positions
- This allowed Jackson to run triangle offense without worrying about defensive mismatches
- Jordan provided perimeter defense while maintaining offensive burden

**Team Defense Philosophy:**
- Rotations built into offensive sets - transition defense was automatic
- Players understood defensive responsibilities because they were integrated into every aspect of practice

## 5. System Over Celebrity: The Revolutionary Approach

What made Jackson different from other coaches:

**1. Managing Star Egos**
- Used triangle offense to prevent Jordan from dominating the ball excessively
- Made superstars accountable within the system structure
- Jordan had to trust teammates, leading to better team chemistry

**2. Position Innovation**
- Created the "point forward" role for Pippen before it was fashionable
- Utilized Rodman's unique skills without forcing offensive responsibility
- Made Kerr a valuable rotational specialist before the 3-point revolution

**3. Practice Preparation**
- Heavy emphasis on repetition and understanding system nuances
- Players knew exactly where to be and what to do in any situation
- This preparation allowed in-game adjustments based on defensive reads

## 6. The Results: Systematic Excellence

**Statistical Dominance Through System:**
- 1995-96: 72-10 record (best ever at the time)
- Every starter understood their role perfectly
- Bench players knew exactly when and how to contribute
- The system worked regardless of individual performance fluctuations

**Sustainable Success:**
- Won three separate three-peats, proving system consistency
- When Jordan retired, the system still worked with different personnel
- Lacked traditional "alpha male" coaching style - let the system do the work

## Key Innovation: The Head Bandage Problem

Jackson's most tactical brilliance was solving the "headband problem" - how to get multiple star players to buy into selflessness. The triangle offense was his solution:

- **Forced ball movement**: No one player could dominate possessions
- **Created interdependence**: Success required everyone executing their role
- **Provided structure**: Gave clear guidelines for decision-making
- **Maximized versatility**: Players could showcase multiple skills within framework

The Bulls' dynasty wasn't just about having great players - it was about having a coach who could systematically maximize each player's strengths while minimizing their weaknesses through tactical innovation. Jackson's triangle offense was essentially a "skills management system" that turned individual excellence into sustainable team dominance.

- 提供身体对抗和篮板保护

<title>Jason Caffey</title>
<fragment>

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Before Caffey could win a third championship ring with the Bulls, he was traded to the Golden State Warriors on February 19, 1998 in exchange for David Vaughn and two second round draft picks.[2] This transaction was not well-received by some of the Bulls' top players, with Michael Jordan stating that "Every time I've seen him (David Vaughn), he's never been in uniform. I think that says a lot," and Dennis Rodman calling it a "dumb" move.[3] Before the beginning of the 1998-99 NBA season, Caffey re-signed with the Warriors on a 7-year, $35 million contract. He averaged career highs of 12.0 points and 6.8 rebounds during the 1999–2000 season with the Warriors.


Caffey joined the Milwaukee Bucks on June 27, 2000, with whom he played three more seasons before his career fizzled out amidst a series of personal problems, including an anxiety attack in 2002[4] and an assault charge in 2003.[5] The Bucks bought out the remaining two seasons ($11.8 million) of his contract before the 2003–04 season started.[6]

<title>Jason Caffey</title>
<fragment>

**Jason Andre Caffey** (born June 12, 1973) is an American former professional basketball player who won two championship rings with the Chicago Bulls in the late 1990s. He later became the head coach of the American Basketball Association's Mobile Bay Hurricanes.




## Basketball career

[edit]

Caffey was born in Mobile, Alabama and played basketball at Davidson High School, where he earned 1st team All State in Class 6A and was named Gatorade's choice for state Player Of The Year.[1] The 6'8" power forward went on to play 4 years at the University of Alabama under coach Wimp Sanderson, and was selected by the Chicago Bulls with the 20th pick of the 1995 NBA draft. He averaged 7.3 points per game during the Bulls' second consecutive championship run in 1996–97. He started 5 playoff games this year, making him one of eleven Chicago Bulls players to start a playoff game amid their championship runs.


</fragment>

Before Caffey could win a third championship ring with the Bulls, he was traded to the Golden State Warriors on February 19, 1998 in exchange for David Vaughn and two second round draft picks.[2] This transaction was not well-received by some of the Bulls' top players, with Michael Jordan stating that "Every time I've seen him (David Vaughn), he's never been in uniform. I think that says a lot," and Dennis Rodman calling it a "dumb" move.[3] Before the beginning of the 1998-99 NBA season, Caffey re-signed with the Warriors on a 7-year, $35 million contract. He averaged career highs of 12.0 points and 6.8 rebounds during the 1999–2000 season with the Warriors.


Caffey joined the Milwaukee Bucks on June 27, 2000, with whom he played three more seasons before his career fizzled out amidst a series of personal problems, including an anxiety attack in 2002[4] and an assault charge in 2003.[5] The Bucks bought out the remaining two seasons ($11.8 million) of his contract before the 2003–04 season started.[6]
